learn.title: Agrivoltaics: Solar Panels and Farming Together
learn.intro: Agrivoltaics combines solar energy generation with agriculture on the same land, maximizing land use efficiency. As India rapidly expands its solar capacity, integrating farming beneath panels offers a sustainable path to meet energy demands while preserving agricultural productivity and supporting rural livelihoods.
learn.c1_text: India has tremendous potential for agrivoltaics given its large agricultural base and growing energy needs. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy is exploring pilot projects to integrate solar with farming, aiming to generate 500 GW of renewable energy by 2030 while safeguarding food security.
learn.c2_text: Solar panels reduce evaporation from soil by up to 33%, conserving water—a critical benefit in drought-prone regions. The panels also protect crops from extreme weather. In arid states like Rajasthan, agrivoltaics could revolutionize water-scarce agriculture while boosting renewable energy output.
learn.stat2: Agrivoltaics can boost crop yields by up to 60%
learn.stat3: Solar panels reduce soil evaporation by up to 33%
learn.stat4: India aims for 500 GW renewable energy by 2030

learn.title: Carbon Markets and Clean Energy Credits
learn.intro: Carbon markets create financial incentives for reducing greenhouse gas emissions through tradable carbon credits. As India commits to net-zero by 2070, these mechanisms play a crucial role in mobilizing private investment for clean energy projects, from solar farms to green manufacturing.
learn.c1_text: Carbon credits represent one ton of CO2 avoided or removed. Companies or countries buy them to offset emissions. Each credit typically costs between $2-20 depending on quality and verification. In India, solar projects earn credits under the Clean Development Mechanism, attracting international investment.
learn.c2_text: Cap-and-trade systems set emission limits and let polluters trade allowances. Carbon taxes directly price emissions. Both encourage clean energy adoption. India's Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme uses tradable energy-saving certificates to improve industrial efficiency across sectors.
learn.c3_text: India launched its national carbon market in 2021 with a target to cut emissions intensity by 45% by 2030. The trading system initially covers 720 units across power and cement sectors. Over 200 million tons of CO2 equivalent were traded in the first phase, showing strong potential for scaling up.
learn.stat1: India: 720 entities covered in national carbon market
learn.stat2: Carbon credits cost $2-20 per ton of CO2
learn.stat3: India aims to cut emissions intensity by 45% by 2030
learn.stat4: Over 200 million tons CO2 traded in India's first phase

learn.title: EV Charging Infrastructure Levels Explained
learn.intro: Understanding EV charging levels is essential as India pushes for 30% electric vehicle adoption by 2030. Different charging speeds affect convenience, range anxiety, and grid planning. From overnight home charging to highway fast-charging corridors, infrastructure determines how smoothly India's EV revolution unfolds.
learn.c1_text: Level 1 uses standard 120V outlets, adding 2-5 miles per hour—too slow for daily commuting. Level 2 uses 240V, adding 10-60 miles per hour. Most Indian homes lack 240V infrastructure, making Level 2 installation crucial for practical EV ownership in urban areas.
learn.c2_text: DC fast chargers bypass onboard chargers, delivering 60-100 kW directly to batteries. They can add 60-100 miles in 20 minutes. India's National Highway Authority plans 5,000 fast-charging stations along highways by 2025 to support long-distance EV travel.
learn.c3_text: India has installed over 140,000 EV charging points as of 2024 under FAME-II scheme. The government plans to install 3.3 million chargers by 2030. Tata Power and IOCL are major players setting up public charging networks in major cities including Delhi, Mumbai, and Bangalore.
learn.stat2: Level 2 adds 10-60 miles per hour of charging
learn.stat4: DC fast chargers add 60-100 miles in 20 minutes

learn.title: Perovskite Solar Cells: Next-Gen Efficiency
learn.intro: Perovskite solar cells promise higher efficiency and lower manufacturing costs than traditional silicon panels. With lab efficiencies exceeding 30%, they could transform India's solar landscape. However, stability and scaling challenges remain before commercial deployment at scale.
learn.c1_text: Perovskite cells achieved 33.7% efficiency in lab tests—surpassing silicon's 26%. Their tunable bandgap allows capturing more sunlight spectrum. They can be printed like ink, reducing production costs by up to 50% compared to silicon manufacturing processes.
learn.c2_text: Perovskites degrade quickly when exposed to moisture and heat. Current modules last only 1-2 years outdoors versus 25+ years for silicon. Researchers are developing encapsulation techniques and tandem cells combining perovskite with silicon to boost both efficiency and durability.
learn.c3_text: IIT Bombay and NREL collaborate on perovskite-silicon tandem cells. India's Solar Energy Corporation plans pilot projects using emerging technologies. If successful, perovskites could reduce solar tariffs below ₹1.5/kWh, making India's 500 GW renewable target more affordable.
learn.stat3: India aims for 500 GW renewable energy by 2030
learn.stat4: Perovskite production could cut costs by 50%

learn.title: Wind Turbine Blades: Lifespan and Recycling
learn.intro: Wind turbine blades last 20-25 years but pose recycling challenges. As India adds 10 GW wind capacity annually, managing end-of-life blades becomes critical. Innovative recycling methods are emerging to convert old blades into construction materials, supporting circular economy goals.
learn.c1_text: Modern wind turbine blades last 20-25 years under normal operation. They endure constant stress from wind forces, requiring regular maintenance including blade inspection every 2-3 years. Offshore turbines face harsher conditions, reducing lifespan to 15-20 years.
learn.c2_text: Blades are mostly fiberglass composite, hard to recycle. New methods include mechanical shredding for cement production, chemical recycling to recover fibers, and blade-to-blade recycling. Global blade waste will reach 43 million tons by 2050 without proper recycling infrastructure.
learn.c3_text: India has 40 GW wind capacity installed, with 15 GW expected to retire by 2030. Suzlon and Vestas are developing blade recycling partnerships. The government's circular economy policy encourages using recycled blade material in road construction and cement manufacturing.
learn.stat2: Blades last 20-25 years under normal use
learn.stat3: 43 million tons of blade waste globally by 2050
learn.stat4: 15 GW of Indian wind capacity to retire by 2030

learn.title: Flow Batteries for Grid-Scale Storage
learn.intro: Flow batteries offer long-duration energy storage crucial for India's renewable integration. Unlike lithium-ion, they can store energy for 10+ hours and last decades. Vanadium and iron-based systems are leading candidates to support India's 500 GW renewable target by 2030.
learn.c1_text: Vanadium flow batteries use liquid electrolytes stored in tanks, offering 20+ year lifespans and unlimited scalability. Iron-based systems are cheaper but less efficient. A 100 MW vanadium system costs $300-500/kWh but provides 10+ hour discharge duration for grid stability.
learn.c2_text: Flow batteries excel at long-duration storage (8-20 hours), complementing short-duration lithium-ion systems. They're ideal for smoothing solar/wind fluctuations and providing backup power. Projects in Australia and California demonstrate 100+ MW installations supporting grid reliability.
learn.c3_text: India plans 4-hour storage mandates for new renewable projects. The government approved 4-hour battery storage tenders worth $2.6 billion. IIT Madras develops low-cost iron-flow batteries. If successful, flow batteries could reduce storage costs below ₹8/kWh, enabling 24x7 renewable power.
learn.stat3: India approved $2.6 billion battery storage tenders
learn.stat4: Flow batteries provide 8-20 hour discharge duration
